{{pagebanner|Fujiya in Ginza Chuo-ku Tokyo Wikivoyage banner.jpg|pgname=Ginza}}

The '''Ginza''' (銀座) district of [[Tokyo]], literally "Silver Mint", is in the [[Tokyo/Chuo|Chuo]] ward.  It is considered the high fashion center of the city and contains many upscale shops and restaurants.

==Get in==

{{Mapframe|35.66934|139.76570|zoom=15}}
{{Mapshape}}

===By train===
Getting to Ginza is easy - in the heart of the area is Ginza station, connected to the Marunouchi (M16), Ginza (G09), and Hibiya (H08) subway lines. Alternatively you may walk to the area from the JR Shimbashi or Yurakucho stations, Higashi-Ginza station on the Toei Asakusa (A11) or the Ginza Itchome station on the Yurakucho (Y19) subway line.

Connections from [[Narita Airport]] can be made either by taking the Keisei line to Ueno, then changing to the Ginza line (¥2,080 and 80 minutes via Keisei's reserved Skyliner service, or ¥1,160 and about 100 minutes via their limited express commuter service), or by JR's Narita Express to Tokyo Station and then the Marunouchi subway (¥2,900, 80 minutes).  Both airport services offer numerous additional connections if your destination is closer to another station.  Domestic passengers flying into [[Haneda|Haneda Airport]] have it easier - Keikyu trains travel directly from the airport to the Asakusa line's Higashi-Ginza station (¥650, 30 minutes).

===By bus===
Airport Limousine Buses run from the airport to major hotels in Ginza, taking 80–90 minutes under normal highway traffic and costing ¥3000.

* The side streets of Ginza are full of '''art galleries''' featuring paintings, photography, and graphic design. The Nichido Garo (日動画廊) near the B9 exit of the Metro Ginza line is one of the most famous, often frequented by collectors from Europe and the United States.
* During '''Christmas''', Ginza's streets are illuminated. 126 trees in Ginzanamiki street are decorated with 75 thousand light bulbs, and 76 trees in Hanatsubaki street are decorated 35 thousand light bulbs which are made in the shape of stars. The illuminations are turned on on November 15.

==Do==
[[File:Saturday in Ginza.jpg|thumb|Saturday on Chuo Dori]]

Weekends on {{marker|type=do|name=Chuo-dori|lat=35.668172|long=139.761833|image=Saturday in Ginza.jpg}} are '''Pedestrians' Paradise''' (歩行者天国), with the street closed to motor traffic during the day. You can catch street music (nothing too loud) and performance, hawkers selling magical puppets which dance without strings, and thousands of other people to bump into.

* {{do
| name=Kabukiza Theater | alt=歌舞伎座 Kabukiza | url=https://www.kabuki-za.co.jp/ | email=
| address=4-12-15 Ginza, near the corner of Showa-dori and Harumi-dori | lat=35.66953 | long=139.768 | directions=underground passage from the Higashi-Ginza station of the Asakusa and Hibiya subway lines
| phone=+81 3-3541-3131 | tollfree= | fax=
| hours= | price=&yen;4000–&yen;20,000
| image=Kabuki-za Theatre 2013 1125.jpg | wikidata=Q3082575
| lastedit=2020-12-30
| content=The best way to see traditional Japanese theater is to go to Kabuki-za for a single act, or ''hitomaku-mi'', which lasts between one and two hours. This costs around &yen;800, depending on the length, and seating is on the fourth floor. An English audio guide describes the play while you watch, it is worthwhile at &yen;700. You can also see the complete kabuki play, but this is a lengthy affair, and ticket prices can range from &yen;4000 to &yen;20,000. If it's around mealtime, pick up a ''bento'' at one of the local shops and take it in. The current Kabukiza Theater opened its doors in 2013, replacing the previous building which stood from 1950 to 2010.
}}
* '''Movie theaters''' are plentiful in the Ginza-Yurakucho area, and as many of them are quite old, they're spacious as well.

==Buy==
Ginza is the home of Tokyo's oldest and most prestigious '''department stores'''; the most exclusive is probably '''Wako'''. And of course Louis Vuitton, Dior, Chanel and Prada have stores as well, as do most other fashion brands you can think of.

==Eat==
[[File:Melonpan (26946924541).jpg|thumb|Digging into a melon-pan]]

'''''Melon-pan''''' (メロンパン ''meronpan''), a fluffy sweet bun with a thick, cookie-like cross-hatched crust, was invented at the nearby Imperial Hotel and is now considered a Ginza icon, with Hotel Okura and Hotel Seiyou famous for their versions.  The name comes from the appearance, and the original recipe had no melon at all, but it's often melon-flavored these days and shops like Kimuraya sell melon-pan in special flavors such as coffee or orange.

* Several cheap restaurants can be found in the alleys northwest of the main intersection (Ginza Yon-chome).  They may be difficult to find as they usually have a plain entrance or they are located in an alley between buildings.

Walk along the sides of the Ginza station and around, there are many cheap places to eat and small places have vending machines and are happy to give you English menus and help out with the vending machine- you just have to ask. They are good places to eat and offer good variety. ¥350-900 for a good curry or bowl of ramen. Look for the little curtains and the sound of cooking!

===Splurge===
Ginza hosts many of Japan's most exclusive (and expensive) ''ryotei'', many of which require not just reservations but introductions before they'll grant you the privilege of paying up to ¥50,000 per person (excluding drinks) for your meal. The following options are somewhat more down to earth and at the very least accept reservations from the general public, provided you have the funds to pay for the meal.

* {{eat
| name=Chikuyōtei | alt=竹葉亭 | url=https://g201100.gorp.jp/ | email=
| address=Ginza 8-14-7 | lat= | long= | directions=Higashi-Ginza stn
| phone=+81 3-3542-0789 | tollfree=
| hours=M-Sa 11:30-14:30, 16:30-20:00 | price=
| content=The original store of Japan's best known ''unagi'' (eel) restaurant chain, serving up luscious ''kabayaki'' (grilled eel with sauce) since 1876. Full courses start from &yen;7350 and climb up to twice that (reservations required), but a basic ''unadon'' with soup is an almost reasonable &yen;2,625.
}}
* {{eat
| name=Ginza Shiseido Parlour | alt=資生堂パーラー | url=http://parlour.shiseido.co.jp/ | email=
| address=Shiseido Bldg 4-5F, Ginza 8-8-3, and several other nearby locations | lat= | long= | directions=
| phone=+81 3-5537-6241 | tollfree=
| hours= | price=
| content=Operated by the cosmetics giant Shiseido, the Parlour (founded 1902) is one of the swankiest places for Japanese-style Western food. Lunch specials go for &yen;4,000, but the most famous item on the menu is the lobster and abalone curry for &yen;10,000.
}}
* {{eat
| name=Sushi Kanesaka | alt=鮨かねさか | url=http://www.sushi-kanesaka.com/ | email=
| address=B1/F Misuzu Bldg, 8-10-3 Ginza Chuou-ku | lat=35.667988 | long=139.762643 | directions=
| phone=+81 3 5568-4411 | tollfree= | fax=
| hours=11:30-13:00, 17:00-22:00 | price=¥5,000 (lunch), ¥20,000 (dinner)
| lastedit=2015-12-21
| content=The main branch of one of Japan's premier sushi restaurants with two Michelin stars, with another branch at the Palace Hotel, as well as two outposts in Singapore. Sushi is prepared fresh for you at the counter while you watch. Ordering dishes individually is not allowed, and the chef would select what he thinks are the best seasonal ingredients for customers. The restaurant is very small with limited seating, so reservations are essential well in advance. Limited English is spoken by the head chef.

There is another restaurant in Ginza that may stand in a class of its own:
* {{eat
| name=Sukiyabashi Jiro | alt=すきやばし次郎 | url=http://www.sushi-jiro.jp/eng-index.html | email=
| address=Tsukamoto Sogyo Building B1F, 2-15, Ginza 4-chome| lat= | long= | directions=
| phone=+81 3 3535-3600 | tollfree= | fax=
| hours=11:30-14:00, 17:30-20:30 (Closed Saturday evenings, Sundays, public holidays, New Year's holiday and mid-August) | price=¥30,000
| lastedit=2016-10-18
| content=This three Michelin star restaurant and its owner/chef, Jiro Ono, were immortalized in the 2011 documentary ''Jiro Dreams of Sushi''. The highly expensive course is ''omakase'' only - Jiro himself selects 20 nigiri pieces daily based on that day's catch from the Tsukiji fish market. You are not expected to use soy sauce, as many pieces are already brushed with it. The restaurant only has ten counter seats, and due to its popularity, advance reservations are required by telephone in Japanese. While reservations open on the first day of every month for the following month's seating, they almost always sell out the same day. Reservations via a concierge (hotel, American Express, etc.) may be the best way for foreign visitors to secure a seat.
}}

==Sleep==
Accommodation in Ginza itself is limited and expensive.  You can shave a fair bit off the price by heading around the corner to [[Tokyo/Shinbashi|Shinbashi]], which is a major train hub and has lots of serviceable mid-range and capsule hotels.

==Go next==

* [[Tokyo/Chiyoda|Tokyo Station]] - the Marunouchi and Yaesu districts around Tokyo Station are a 20-minute walk north of Ginza's center
* [[Tokyo/Chiyoda|Yurakucho]] - west of Ginza, this area houses a mix of commercial and reasonable shopping compared to Ginza's high end areas
* [[Tokyo/Chuo|Hama-Rikyu Detached Palace Garden]] - south of the Ginza, these former Imperial pleasure gardens are an oasis of tranquility in a hectic city. Here you can catch a tour boat which will take you up the Sumida River to Asakusa. From the river, much of the Tokyo skyline is visible.
* [[Tokyo/Chuo|Tsukiji]] - south-east of Ginza, this area is famous for the "outer market" of former wholesale fish market.
* [[Tokyo/Chiyoda|Hibiya Park]] - just west of Ginza past the Sony Building and elevated highway, this park contains many different European styles. In May/June, the azaleas are in bloom.
* [[Tokyo/Chiyoda|Imperial Palace]] - just north of Hibiya Park, making it an easy walk from Ginza.  Enjoy the open parks and venture a little into the public park area.
